title: A Vow for the Summer
premise: Orsen Marchetti, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter and part-time novelist, has spent ten years avoiding the town of Saltmere and the boy who betrayed her family's claim to the Marchetti light. When the local library's anonymous pen-pal program pairs her with a stranger, the letters grow intimate — until she discovers her correspondent is Theo Vance, the man whose testimony cost her grandfather everything. As Orsen weighs loyalty to her family against the truth emerging in his letters, a storm season threatens both the decommissioned lighthouse and the deadline for an inheritance that could restore it. In the end, Orsen must speak the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade — a public truth that clears her grandfather's name, costs her the family's approval, and finally lets her love in the present tense.
about_author: Rosalind Voss is the pen name of a former court stenographer who traded transcripts for tide charts and now writes romance from a rented cottage on the Atlantic coast. Her novels are known for slow-burning letters, stubborn heroines, and justice that arrives one confession at a time.

chapters.title: The Light Nobody Tends
chapters.summary: Orsen returns to Saltmere for her grandmother's funeral, cataloguing the decaying lighthouse she swore never to see again. Through her eyes we learn the family lost the keeper's post after a falsified safety report ten years ago. Emotional beat: grief braided with old resentment; she plans to sell and leave within the month.

chapters.title: Strangers by Assignment
chapters.summary: Hiding from well-meaning neighbors in the library, Orsen is roped into the winter pen-pal program by her childhood friend Priya. She writes a guarded first letter under a pseudonym. Beat: reluctant vulnerability; writing to a stranger feels safer than speaking to anyone who knows her name.

chapters.title: Yours, Anonymously
chapters.summary: Theo Vance, now the county's youngest magistrate clerk, receives the assignment and answers with disarming honesty about guilt he won't name. His POV reveals he recognized something in the handwriting-adjacent phrasing but dismisses the thought. Beat: two people telling truths they can't say aloud.

chapters.title: Terms of the Estate
chapters.summary: A lawyer reads the will: the lighthouse passes to Orsen only if she resides there through the summer solstice and reopens it for one public season. Her uncle Marcus, who brokered the original sale, objects furiously. Beat: Orsen trapped between escape and obligation; she stays out of spite.

chapters.title: The Man at the Hearing Room
chapters.summary: Orsen encounters Theo at a coastal zoning hearing where he represents the county against her lighthouse exemption. Their hostility is instant and personal, though neither knows why the other seems familiar. Beat: enemies established on paper before intimacy blooms in ink.

chapters.title: Letters Like Confession
chapters.summary: The correspondence deepens: her correspondent admits he once helped destroy someone's livelihood and has spent years unable to undo it. Orsen, moved, confesses her own exile without naming Saltmere. Beat: dramatic irony tightens as each recognizes pieces of the other's story.

chapters.title: Salt in the Walls
chapters.summary: Restoring the lighthouse alone, Orsen finds her grandfather's hidden logbooks suggesting the safety violation was fabricated. Marcus warns her to stop digging. Beat: the past stops being abstract; grief curdles into purpose.

chapters.title: What Theo Knew
chapters.summary: Theo's POV: as a nineteen-year-old intern, he transcribed testimony he was pressured to alter, and his silence bought his career. He begins investigating the old case through official channels. Beat: guilt becomes action; he starts pulling threads that lead toward Orsen's family.

chapters.title: Midsummer Fair, Midsummer Lie
chapters.summary: Town festival forces Orsen and Theo onto the same committee. Banter sharpens into reluctant respect; almost-tenderness interrupted by Marcus's pointed reminder of what the Vances cost the Marchettis. Beat: attraction denied at the threshold.

chapters.title: The Handwriting on Page Nine
chapters.summary: Theo, rereading his pen-pal's letters, matches a distinctive phrase to a zoning appeal Orsen filed. He suspects but doesn't confirm, terrified of losing the one honest relationship he has. Beat: dread and longing entwined; he keeps writing anyway.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: An early hurricane damages the lighthouse roof days before inspection. Theo arrives unasked with tarps and labor. Working side by side, they nearly cross the line from adversaries to something else. Beat: tenderness under pressure; Orsen softens against her will.

chapters.title: The Logbook and the Letter
chapters.summary: Orsen mails her pen pal a photograph of the forged report, asking how such a thing could happen in a just system. Theo realizes the document is the one he altered. Beat: full recognition; he must decide whether to confess or disappear.

chapters.title: Confession, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Theo writes back admitting everything except his name, enclosing the original unaltered transcript he kept for ten years. Orsen reads it by lamplight and understands her pen pal is her enemy. Beat: betrayal layered atop betrayal; she burns to confront him.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Wick Room
chapters.summary: Orsen traps Theo at the lighthouse and reveals she knows both identities. He begs for the chance to testify formally; she accuses him of comforting her under false pretenses. Beat: the midpoint rupture; raw, mutual, unforgiving.

chapters.title: Marcus's Bargain
chapters.summary: Marcus offers Orsen a clean sale if she drops the investigation, revealing he was paid to look away a decade ago. Loyalty to family now means accepting the lie. Beat: the theme crystallizes — loyalty versus truth, and which one is actually betrayal.

chapters.title: The Testimony He Prepared
chapters.summary: Theo files to reopen the case, risking disbarment for his youthful misconduct. His POV shows him choosing ruin over comfort, mailing Orsen a final letter asking nothing but a hearing attendance. Beat: atonement without expectation of forgiveness.

chapters.title: What the Family Wants
chapters.summary: Orsen's mother arrives, pleading with her to let the dead rest and take the money. The rehearsed sentence — the truth about the forgery — sits on Orsen's tongue. Beat: lowest point; every path costs someone she loves.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Climax. Before the review board, Theo testifies to the alteration and presents the original transcript. Called forward, Orsen finally speaks the sentence she rehearsed for ten years, naming the forgery publicly despite Marcus and her mother in the room. Beat: catharsis through courage; the truth lands like a struck bell.

chapters.title: After the Verdict
chapters.summary: The keeper's post and deed are restored pending appeal; Marcus walks out of the family; her mother, shaken, begins her own reckoning. Orsen and Theo stand apart, unspeakably changed, forgiveness not yet granted. Beat: justice achieved, love unresolved.

chapters.title: The Last Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Orsen writes the pen pal she no longer has — a letter forgiving the boy he was, addressed to the man she might love. Theo, reading his copy of her earlier letters, comes to the lighthouse at dusk. Beat: hope rekindled cautiously, on honest ground.

chapters.title: First Light
chapters.summary: On the summer solstice, Orsen relights the lamp for the first public season as required by the will. Theo stands beside her, introduced to the town plainly, no pseudonyms left. Beat: quiet joy; identity and love finally aligned.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Epilogue in letters and journal entries across the following year: the appeal upheld, Orsen's novel about a lighthouse and a liar finished, a new letter arriving that needs no anonymity. Beat: resolution — she loves in the present tense, and signs her own name.
